passage:
Club diary, Vinita, teacher-in-charge of the film club.
At Thursday's meeting Urmila spoke for most of the hour: the short-film idea, her cousin's camera, a trip to the coast. She did not ask anyone a question. I watched the others. Faiz began drawing in the margin of a notebook. Two students checked their phones under the table. Meera, who had brought three story ideas last month, stopped offering any. Urmila did not seem to notice at all.
I did not call Urmila out in front of the group. After the meeting I asked, "Which of the others' ideas stayed with you today?" Urmila paused for a long moment. Next week I will try a round where each person speaks for one minute.

qa.q: Who stopped offering story ideas at the Thursday meeting?
qa.a: Meera, who had brought three story ideas the month before.

qa.q: What was Vinita worried about while watching the group?
qa.a: That the quieter members were disengaging quietly, while Urmila seemed not to notice.

qa.q: What did Vinita choose to do instead of calling Urmila out in front of the group?
qa.a: Vinita asked Urmila privately which of the others' ideas had stayed with Urmila, and planned a one-minute round for next week.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel when asked which of the others' ideas stayed with her?
qa.a: Possibly surprised or a little embarrassed, then thoughtful. The long pause suggests Urmila had not been listening for the others' ideas and began to notice.

grounding: A group notices one member who takes the floor and rarely asks anything back, while others quietly disengage.

passage:
Saturday night. Lunch with my friends again, and Payal did nearly all the talking, first about her cousin's wedding photographs, then about her exam predictions. She never asked Tanya a single thing back. I watched. Tanya turned the water bottle around and around. Ishaan started scrolling. I opened my mouth twice and closed it twice. I like Payal, she's funny and generous, and I'm pretty sure she has no idea. I don't know what to do. Maybe next time I'll ask Tanya a small question in a gap, like "Did you finish the sketch?", and see whether Payal follows. If it keeps happening, maybe I'll tell Payal kindly, when it's just the two of us.
Mahima

qa.q: What did Tanya do while Payal talked?
qa.a: Tanya turned the water bottle around and around.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling about speaking up at lunch?
qa.a: Torn and unsure. Mahima likes Payal and wants to include Tanya, but opened and closed the mouth twice without speaking.

qa.q: What small step does Mahima plan to try next time?
qa.a: To ask Tanya a small question in a gap, like whether the sketch is finished, and see whether Payal follows.

qa.q: How might Payal see the lunch?
qa.a: Probably as an enjoyable chat. Mahima is pretty sure Payal has no idea the others are losing interest.

grounding: A friend notices one person always takes the floor, others disengage, and the dominant person is unaware.

passage: Every evening at the bus stand in Palampur, the same five teenagers gathered after tuition. And every evening, Hemant talked. About his cousin's bike, the hill race, his plan to become a pilot. Neelam started counting one day. In forty minutes, Hemant didn't ask a single question. When Rupa tried to tell them about her grandmother's recovery, Hemant cut in: "Speaking of hospitals, my uncle—" Rupa stopped talking. Over the next week, Neelam noticed the others arriving later, checking phones, leaving early. Deepak started taking the earlier bus. Hemant didn't seem to notice anything. He just talked louder to the three who remained. Neelam felt sorry for him and annoyed at once. On Friday she caught him alone. "Hemant, Rupa never finished her story about her grandmother." Hemant blinked. "She didn't?"

qa.q: How long did Neelam count Hemant talking without asking a question?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling about Hemant by Friday?
qa.a: She felt sorry for him and annoyed at once, seeing that his talking was driving friends away.

qa.q: What did Neelam do that might help Hemant?
qa.a: She spoke to him alone and gently pointed out one specific moment, Rupa's unfinished story, instead of criticising him in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Hemant see the bus-stand evenings?
qa.a: He seems to think they're going fine, not noticing that friends are arriving late and leaving early.

grounding: Shows a group of friends where one person always takes the floor and rarely asks back, while others quietly disengage without him noticing.

passage: At lunch in their Madrid school, Diego always took the head of the table and the whole conversation with it. Football, his summer in Portugal, the video game he was best at. Lucia had been watching for a week. When Sofia said her parents were splitting up, Diego said, "That's rough. Anyway, did you see the match?" Sofia looked at her tray. The next day, Sofia ate in the library. Two others followed. Diego complained, "Where is everybody?" but didn't seem to wonder why. Lucia felt uneasy. She liked Diego. He was funny and kind in his way. On Thursday she said to him quietly, walking to class, "Sofia told us something big on Monday. Did you notice she didn't finish?" Diego stopped. "I... didn't." He was quiet for a few steps. "Should I ask her about it?"

qa.q: What did Diego say after Sofia's news?
qa.a: He said, 'That's rough. Anyway, did you see the match?'

qa.q: What was Lucia feeling as friends began leaving the table?
qa.a: Lucia felt uneasy, liking Diego but seeing how his talking was pushing others away.

qa.q: What small step did Lucia take, and why was it well chosen?
qa.a: She mentioned Sofia's unfinished news to Diego privately while walking, which let him realise it himself without being embarrassed in front of others.

qa.q: How might Sofia have felt when Diego changed the subject?
qa.a: Sofia was probably hurt and unheard, looking at her tray and then eating in the library.

grounding: Shows a group of teenagers where one friend dominates and rarely asks anything back, while others quietly disengage without him noticing.

passage: In the hostel common room, Harish was on his fourth story in a row: the district quiz, the cousin in Canada, the time he fixed the warden's phone. Sunaina counted. In twenty minutes nobody else had finished a sentence. When Meenal began, "My mother called today, she—", Harish cut in: "Oh, mine too, listen to this." Meenal stopped. Sunaina watched the circle shrink: Jaspreet picked up her phone, Arun drifted over to the carrom board, and Meenal went quiet and picked at a nail. Harish laughed at his own punchline and didn't seem to notice anyone had gone. Sunaina felt a flash of irritation, then something closer to pity. Later, walking to the mess, she asked Meenal, "What were you going to say about your mother?"

qa.q: Where did Arun drift off to?
qa.a: He drifted over to the carrom board.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she watched the circle shrink?
qa.a: She felt a flash of irritation at Harish, then something closer to pity that he didn't notice everyone leaving.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say to Harish another day?
qa.a: When they are alone, she could tell him kindly that others rarely get to finish, and suggest he ask one question back before his next story.

qa.q: What was it like for Meenal when Harish cut in?
qa.a: She probably felt brushed aside and discouraged, so she stopped talking and picked at a nail.

grounding: Shows a teenager noticing a peer who always takes the floor while the others quietly disengage and he does not notice.
